title: THEY DON'T NEED YOUR NAME
subtitle: THE GRAPH CAN FIND YOU FIRST.

blocks.text: A BLOCKCHAIN ADDRESS DOES NOT NEED YOUR NAME ATTACHED TO IT TO START REVEALING STRUCTURE.
PSEUDONYMOUS IS NOT ANONYMOUS.

A Bitcoin-style address is a pseudonym. The ledger does not normally print a legal name beside it, but it does publish transactions that can be analyzed as a graph. The question for an observer becomes less 'What is this person's name?' and more 'Which pieces of this graph appear to belong together?'
01 // CO-SPENDING

A classic technique is the common-input or co-spend heuristic. When several UTXOs are consumed together in an ordinary transaction, analysts may infer common control. This can connect addresses that looked unrelated before the spend.

It is a heuristic, not a universal law. Collaborative transaction designs such as CoinJoin can deliberately violate the assumption. That limitation is important: clustering produces evidence and inference, not omniscience.
02 // CHANGE

Bitcoin transactions often create change. If an analyst can identify which output is likely change, that output can extend the suspected wallet cluster into the next transaction. Script types, amount patterns and wallet behavior have all been used as clues.
ONE TRANSACTION CAN CREATE A CLUE. REPEATED WALLET BEHAVIOR CAN TURN CLUES INTO A MAP.
03 // LABELS

Clustering becomes much more useful when part of the graph receives a real-world label. Exchanges, merchants, donation addresses, public posts and other off-chain records can provide attribution points. A label attached to one portion of a cluster can change how surrounding historical activity is interpreted.
04 // PATTERNS

Timing, recurring transfers, consolidation, peeling chains and characteristic wallet behavior can add context. None of these signals should automatically be treated as proof of identity. Analysis is strongest when multiple independent signals agree and weakest when a heuristic is stretched beyond its assumptions.
THE IMPORTANT LIMITATION

Blockchain analytics can be wrong. Common-input ownership can fail in collaborative transactions. Change detection can be ambiguous. Labels can be incomplete or incorrect. A responsible description of graph analysis must preserve that uncertainty rather than pretending every line on a visualization represents a known person.
THE GRAPH IS POWERFUL. IT IS NOT MAGIC.
WHAT SHIELDED ZCASH CHANGES

Fully shielded Zcash does not expose the protected sender address, recipient address and amount as a transparent transaction graph. That removes much of the raw payment structure that ordinary address clustering depends on. The network verifies validity cryptographically instead of requiring those payment details to be public.

This does not make a user invisible. Zcash documentation warns that metadata, network-layer observation and transparent interactions can still create correlations. Privacy has layers, and shielded cryptography protects the payment layer rather than every possible source of information.
THE DIFFERENCE IN ONE LINE.
PSEUDONYMOUS IS NOT THE SAME THING AS UNKNOWN.
